title: Love your enemies
hookLine: love your enemies, pray for them that persecute you

lines: AND THE PERSON WHO HURT YOU.
cards: Loving a friend is easy to admire. Loving a stranger, as this block heard a few days ago, takes some work.
But there's often someone in a life who is neither: the coworker who undermined you, the relative who keeps score, the ex, the neighbor with the leaf blower and the grudge.
On a mountain in Galilee, in the teaching Christians call the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus names that person directly. He doesn't say tolerate them, or avoid them, or forgive them eventually.
He says something that sounds almost impossible.

teach.b: The King James puts it like this: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you," and the verse goes on: pray for those who mistreat and persecute you.
First, the verbs: love, bless, do good, pray. None is a feeling you have to fake; each is something a person can do while the hurt is still there. Second, the reason.

teach.h: SUN ON THE EVIL AND ON THE GOOD.
teach.b: God, Jesus says, "maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust." The sunrise doesn't check anyone's record, and neither does the rain.
To love an enemy, in this teaching, is to be a little like that: given to everyone. Third, the roots. This isn't a break with the scripture Jesus grew up with.
Proverbs already says, "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat." Jesus takes up that thread and carries it on, from bread to blessing to prayer. Fourth, the Gospels show him doing it.
In Luke, from the cross, he prays for the men crucifying him: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Christians apply this in different ways.

Some traditions, like the Mennonites and the Quakers, read it as a call to refuse violence altogether; other churches read it as a command about the heart and daily conduct that still leaves room for defending the innocent.
Love here isn't approval. It's wanting good for someone who doesn't want good for you.

how: Christians pray for people they find difficult, sometimes by name in private prayer, and some churches include prayers for enemies or for those who wish them harm in their regular worship.

o: love that wants good for others, even enemies
the fond, warm love between family members
a feeling of liking someone you already know

games.q: inside the teaching — tap the pairs.
p: rises on the evil and on the good
if thine enemy be hungry, give bread

s: loving your enemies means pretending they did nothing wrong
the verbs are acts: love, bless, do good, pray. none requires approval.
the idea of feeding your enemy already appears in Proverbs
"If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat."
every church reads this command the same way
some traditions read it as refusing violence; others as a command about the heart and daily conduct.

games.q: someone has been cursing you behind your back, and they're still at it. according to the Sermon on the Mount, what do you do?
o: cut them off and say nothing.
bless them, and pray for them.
wait until they apologize, then forgive.
games.why: bless them that curse you, and pray for them. no waiting for an apology: the sun rises on the evil and on the good.

practice: Let one difficult person come to mind, not the worst one, someone you can picture without your stomach knotting completely, and let whatever rises, anger, hurt, tiredness, simply be there.
Then slowly wish them one ordinary good thing: sleep tonight, a day without pain, someone who is kind to them. You don't have to mean it perfectly, and if you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Agape. The love Jesus commands even for enemies: bless them, do good to them, pray for them, like the sun that rises on everyone. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: love your enemies, with a form of the same word, agape, as God is love.

carryVoice: Your line: even them. Wanting their good, without pretending the hurt away. Until tomorrow, then.
